prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Operating and Financial Metrics (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 82px · one-line width 407px
  col 2: header "FY 2022" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 61px
  col 3: header "FY 2023" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 62px
  col 4: header "FY 2024" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 61px
  col 5: header "Q1 2025" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 63px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"bad","why":"Metric column squeezed to ~75px, so row labels break mid-word (\"revenu e retenti on\", \"blende d\", \"month s\") and numbers split too (\"$318.4 M\"); the table fits the box but is unreadable and comparison across years is destroyed."},"B":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Row labels wrap at word boundaries (4 lines) but numeric columns are too tight: headers break (\"FY\"/\"2022\") and amounts split from their unit (\"$318.4\"/\"M\"), and the Q1 2025 column is sliced in half at the edge with its header cut (\"Q1 20…\")."},"C":{"grade":"good","why":"Clean word-level wrapping in the metric column, one-line headers, and values like \"$318.4M\" stay intact; cost is that FY 2024 is cut mid-column at the edge, so the reader scrolls without a clean stopping point."},"D":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Similar to B — 4-5 line row labels, one-line values for most rows, but \"FY 2024\" header wraps to two lines inconsistently and the Q1 column is cut through its header and values, reading as accidental clipping."},"E":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Best balance: metric column wide enough for tidy 3-4 line wraps at word boundaries, all three visible year headers on one line, every number intact (\"$318.4M\", \"$92.5M\"), and the edge falls exactly on the FY 2024 column boundary so the hidden Q1 column is a clean continuation rather than a sliced column."},"F":{"grade":"good","why":"Widest metric column gives the most readable row labels (2-3 lines) and keeps numbers whole, but it buys that by pushing FY 2024 and Q1 off-screen, so only two of four data columns are fully usable per screen."}},"best":["E"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"Whether a partially peeking column (C) should count as a helpful scroll affordance rather than a flaw, and whether F's wider label column is preferable if most reading is vertical (row-by-row) rather than across years."}
